content.text: I'm thinking through how to approach this.

Anscombe and Tukey (1963) provide a methodological basis for using residuals to diagnose offsets and model fit problems. Anscombe (1973) illustrates the importance of residual analysis for detecting systematic model errors, referencing Anscombe's quartet. This includes both fitted error and prediction. The survey of influential observations by Chatterjee and Hadi (1986) provides additional context.

The *Statistical Science* papers detail critical distinctions within model diagnostics. One paper reviews regression diagnostics, residual decompositions, and error analysis. Another elucidates the difference between in-sample model fitting versus out-of-sample predictive evaluation. The *Journal of the American Statistical Association* paper connects in-sample error and true prediction error using covariance penalties. *Statistics Surveys* reviews estimating prediction error versus training error. The *Journal of the American Statistical Association* piece outlines how regression residuals affect the shift in parameter estimates.

Initial focus is on foundational papers that define residuals and their role in identifying systematic prediction errors.  Specifically, Cox and Snell (1968) provides a general definition of residuals to assess departures from fitted predictions. Breiman (2001) contrasts data modeling versus algorithmic modeling, highlighting the difference between in-sample and out-of-sample evaluations. Stone (1974) introduces cross-validation for contrasting training errors with predictive performance.

Reviewing additional papers provides context on residual analysis. "Assumption-Lean Regression" offers an educational reframing of linear regression, highlighting how offsets and misspecified predictors impact fitted errors. "Exploratory Data Analysis for Complex Models" frames residual diagnostics as a comparison between fitted expectations and empirical observations. "Models as Approximations I" analyzes linear regression under model misspecification, demonstrating systematic deviations from true response surfaces.
